title: Twistor revival: helical-anisotropy Fe-Al nanowire memory, platinum-free
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1957 twistor: electroplate an Fe-Al (Alfenol) or NiFe shell on copper nanowires while a mismatched coaxial stress layer applies torsion, locking in a helical easy axis. Bits are helical magnetization segments switched by coincident wire current and an orthogonal copper strap, and read inductively along the same wire, so no MTJ stack is needed.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes the Pt/Ir/Ru/Ta layers of MRAM and the Hf/W of DRAM; magnetic storage gives unlimited endurance and zero refresh energy (fact 3); claims a 30-60 ns cycle with ~10x less scarce metal per bit.

title: Plated-wire NDRO cells on copper bitlines, read without destroying data
idea: Revive 1960s aerospace plated-wire memory: electroplate a 20 nm NiFeCo sheath with circumferential anisotropy around damascene copper bitlines in BEOL, with aluminum word straps crossing over. A word pulse tilts the sheath magnetization without flipping it, so the sign of the induced bitline voltage gives the bit non-destructively. Aqueous plating at <80 C needs no W, no high-k and no fluorinated etch.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): only addressed bits are sensed and nothing is restored; avoids W, Hf and PFAS etch gases; nonvolatile, so no refresh; claims ~3x lower read energy per useful bit.

title: Thin-film transfluxor cells that compute while reading, ferrite-only materials
idea: Revive RCA's 1956 transfluxor: sputter NiZn-ferrite rings with one large and one small aperture in BEOL. The stored blocked/unblocked flux state of the outer leg decides whether a drive on the small aperture induces an output, giving non-destructive read plus AND/inhibit logic in the same element, so rows can be filtered before any data leaves the array.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and overfetch (fact 8) through in-place filtering; built only from Fe, Ni, Zn, O and Cu (no Hf, W, Pt or In); claims 5-10x less data shipped for scan and filter workloads.

title: Drum-style lockstep weight broadcast replaces replicated HBM weight copies
idea: Revive the magnetic-drum principle, where data circulates past many fixed heads: keep ONE copy of model weights in a pod-level pool and stream it every token step over a DWDM optical broadcast (passive 1:64 splitters). All inference replicas consume the same rotating stream in lockstep and hold only a small sliding window locally. A 100 GB model at 50 steps/s needs ~40 Tb/s, about four 100-channel fibers.
why: Uses less of the scarce resource, DRAM itself: replicated-serving pods keep up to 64 identical weight copies in HBM, and broadcasting frees 40-70% of HBM capacity for KV cache, like adding supply without any wafers.

title: Eccles-Jordan flip-flop rebuilt from nanoscale vacuum-channel triodes
idea: Revive the 1918 vacuum-tube flip-flop at nanometer scale: cross-couple two field-emission vacuum-channel triodes (silicon tips, 50 nm sealed gaps, no gate dielectric) into a static latch. The vacuum gap has no dielectric leakage and no junctions, so the cell holds state without refresh and runs at 250 C.
why: Removes Hf/Zr dielectrics, implants and the leakage tail (fact 3); running hot lets data centers drop chillers, saving energy and water; claims refresh energy near zero.

title: Bubble memory reborn in manganese nitride with on-chip rotating fields
idea: Revive Bobeck's 1970s bubble memory without Gd/Ga garnet substrates: sputter perpendicular ferrimagnetic Mn4N on silicon, pattern permalloy asymmetric-disk propagation tracks, and drive every bubble with a 100 MHz rotating in-plane field from quadrature on-chip striplines. One global drive replaces per-cell transistors, and each minor loop needs just one magnetoresistive detector.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and scarce inputs: no gadolinium/gallium (China-dominated), no Hf or W, nonvolatile; a cheap nonvolatile spill tier for cold pages cuts DRAM per server; claims 3-5x lower cost per bit than DRAM.

title: Anderson's 1952 crossbar ferroelectric memory revived in hafnium-free AlBN
idea: Revive J.R. Anderson's transistor-less barium-titanate crossbar store using wurtzite aluminum-boron-nitride ferroelectric films (all abundant elements). Anderson's V/3 half-select scheme is combined with pulse shaping that exploits AlBN's very square loop to suppress disturb, and rows are read by switching current and then rewritten.
why: No hafnium/zirconium and no transistor per cell, which cuts periphery and scarce inputs; a 4F2 crossbar stacks in BEOL; the honest risk is endurance (1e6-1e9), so it serves as a nonvolatile working tier behind DRAM caches; claims 2x density at the same node.

title: MEMS parametrons store bits as oscillation phase, no leakage tail
idea: Revive Eiichi Goto's 1954 parametron with AlN-on-silicon micro-resonators pumped at twice their natural frequency. Each resonator settles into a 0 or pi phase state that persists as long as the shared pump runs, and is read by phase comparison with a reference line.
why: Retention depends on a shared resonant pump (Q~1e4), not on leakage, so the refresh tail disappears (fact 3); uses only Al, N and Si (no Hf, W or In); fits refresh-free scratchpads next to accelerators.

title: MgB2 persistor arrays: niobium-free cryogenic memory without liquid helium
idea: Revive the 1957 persistor (a persistent supercurrent loop) and Buck's cryotron in magnesium diboride (Tc 39 K): bits are clockwise or counterclockwise currents in MgB2 loops switched by thermal cryotron gates. The arrays run at 20-25 K on sealed pulse-tube coolers rather than liquid-helium baths.
why: Avoids consuming helium (Qatar outage) and the niobium chokepoint of SFQ memory (~85% from one Brazilian producer); zero-resistance loops need no refresh; claims 10-100x lower energy per access for cryogenic AI and quantum controllers.

title: Si-only Esaki tunnel-diode latch replaces the DRAM capacitor
idea: Revive TI's 1990s tunneling SRAM, descended from Esaki's 1957 diode: stack two delta-doped, silicon-only interband tunnel diodes (no germanium) on the storage node of a single access transistor. The negative-differential-resistance pair latches the node at two stable voltages, giving a static cell with pA-level standby current and no capacitor.
why: Removes the high-aspect-ratio capacitor (fact 1), its ZrO2/HfO2 and its TiN/W electrodes, and refresh (fact 3); claims a static cell with a 1T footprint of ~8F2.

title: Zuse Z1 mechanical memory shrunk to buckled silicon-carbide nanobeams
idea: Revive Konrad Zuse's 1938 sheet-metal mechanical memory as NEMS: a SiC nanobeam pre-buckled by residual stress snaps between up and down states under electrostatic pull and is read capacitively without switching. Because the state is mechanical geometry, no charge can leak away.
why: Zero leakage means no refresh (fact 3); uses only Si, C and N (no Hf, W or Ta); tolerates heat and radiation; claims nonvolatile working memory with ~10 ns switching, with endurance of 1e12+ cycles as the honest risk.

title: Widrow memistor revival: electroplated analog weights in solid electrolyte
idea: Revive Bernard Widrow's 1960 memistor, a three-terminal cell that plates copper onto a carbon resistor: use a PFAS-free copper-doped phosphosilicate-glass electrolyte so a separate write terminal plates or strips copper while the read terminal senses resistance. Each cell holds a 6-bit analog weight and multiplies in place.
why: One cell replaces six DRAM bits of frozen weights and computes in situ (fact 5); uses only Cu, C, P and Si; separate read and write paths give unlimited read endurance; claims 4-6x fewer DRAM bits for inference weights.

title: Adiabatic resonant wordline drivers recycle charge, reviving 1990s reversible computing
idea: Revive 1990s adiabatic switching (Younis/Knight) for DRAM periphery: drive wordlines and plate lines from shared on-die LC tanks with slow sinusoidal ramps, so each activation's charge returns to the tank instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers 50-70% of the 3 V wordline CV2 energy, and energy is a scarce data-center resource; needs no new materials.

title: ThruChip inductive coupling revived to strip signal TSVs from HBM
idea: Revive Kuroda's abandoned ThruChip Interface: replace the thousands of signal TSVs in an HBM stack with on-die spiral coils that couple data inductively between thinned dies, keeping only a few coarse, wide-pitch power TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): frees TSV keep-out area and copper fill and removes a major yield detractor; claims 1.5-2x more HBM bits per wafer.

title: 1990s BST capacitor revived with US-molybdenum SrMoO3 electrodes
idea: Revive the abandoned gigabit-era barium-strontium-titanate capacitor (k~200-300) using conductive perovskite SrMoO3 electrodes, with molybdenum mined in Colorado, instead of Pt/Ru. The dielectric grows lattice-matched without a low-k dead layer.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): k~200 gives 5 fF at an aspect ratio of ~20 instead of 70, removing Hf/Zr, Ru/Pt and much of the deep fluorocarbon etch; claims ~30% fewer cell process steps.

title: Cultured-quartz program revived: fully synthetic silica crucibles from SiCl4
idea: Copy the WWII Signal Corps/Bell Labs move that replaced Brazilian natural quartz with hydrothermally cultured crystal: make the whole Czochralski crucible, not just its inner layer, from flame-hydrolysed synthetic silica soot made from silicon tetrachloride, a by-product of US polysilicon plants.
why: Breaks the Spruce Pine (>80%) chokepoint for high-purity quartz crucibles and turns a waste stream into feedstock; claims full crucible supply independence for US wafer makers.

title: Soviet cold-crucible skull melting for crucible-free Czochralski silicon
idea: Revive Soviet-era cold-crucible induction melting: hold the silicon melt in a water-cooled, segmented copper crucible where a frozen silicon skull forms the container, then pull Czochralski ingots from it, adding oxygen by gas doping for gettering.
why: Removes quartz crucibles (Spruce Pine) and their per-pull consumption entirely; copper and water are abundant; claims zero crucible spend, at the cost of ~2x melt energy.

title: Audio-RAM revival: sell partially defective DRAM for tolerant AI workloads
idea: Revive 1980s ARAM, defective DRAM sold for answering machines: bin HBM/DDR dies that fail full spec, burn their bad-row maps into on-die fuses/SPD, and sell them for error-tolerant KV cache and low-precision activation storage, with the OS/runtime retiring the mapped rows.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: HBM yield loss is 20-30%, and recovering half of it raises usable bits per wafer 10-15% with no new capacity.

title: Wartime salvage drive for DRAM: harvest chips from retired servers
idea: Revive WWII scrap-salvage logistics for memory: collect DDR4/DDR5 modules from decommissioned servers, robotically desolder and re-ball the packages, burn-in and retest them, and rebuild them onto CXL memory-expander cards pooled as a slower tier.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: millions of server DIMMs are shredded every year, and reuse adds supply with zero wafers, helium or quartz; claims several percent of annual bit demand.

title: Re-establish the Federal Helium Reserve with mandatory fab helium recapture
idea: Reverse the 2024 sale of the Amarillo Bush Dome reserve: restore a federal helium reserve with semiconductor priority, and revive the 1960 Helium Act's conservation intent by requiring fabs to recapture backside-cooling and leak-test helium with on-site purifiers and liquefiers.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar's ~30% offline since March 2026): recapture cuts fab helium purchases 70-90% and the reserve buffers outages.

title: 1970s molybdenum-gate MOS revived to replace tungsten wordlines
idea: Revive molybdenum-gate MOS, and the WWII practice of substituting molybdenum for tungsten: fill buried wordlines and bitline contacts with barrier-thin Mo deposited from MoCl5/MoO2Cl2 instead of WF6, sourced from US mines.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and fluorine use (WF6): Mo's short electron mean free path lowers narrow-line resistance; claims near-zero tungsten per wafer.

title: Intel 1103 three-transistor cell rebuilt in indium-free zinc-tin oxide
idea: Revive the 1970 Intel 1103 3T dynamic cell in BEOL-stacked amorphous zinc-tin-oxide transistors, with no indium and no gallium. The wide bandgap gives ultra-low off-current, so the gate node holds charge for seconds and the gain transistor reads it non-destructively.
why: The prior work's IGZO depends on indium and gallium, both concentrated in China, while ZTO uses Zn and Sn; the gain read removes the capacitor (fact 1), slashes refresh (fact 3) and stacks over the periphery (fact 7).

title: Dry cleaning revival: vapor HF and UV-ozone replace wet benches
idea: Revive 1990s anhydrous HF/alcohol vapor oxide etching and UV-ozone organic removal for a large share of the 100+ wet clean steps in a DRAM flow, keeping RCA wet cleans only where particles demand them.
why: Water and energy: DRAM fabs use millions of gallons of ultrapure water a day; claims a 30-40% cut in ultrapure water and less chemical waste.

title: Williams tube reborn: microcolumn e-beams write charge on blank plates
idea: Revive the 1947 Williams-Kilburn tube: an i-line-patterned array of field-emission microcolumns at 2 um pitch, in a sealed MEMS vacuum, each steers a ~10 nm spot over a 200x200-bit patch of an UNPATTERNED SiO2/Si3N4 storage plate. The beams write charge and read it back by secondary-emission current, so bit density comes from the beam spot, not from lithography.
why: No EUV and almost no patterning of the storage medium (fact 4: capital); no capacitors, Hf or W; claims a 10 nm bit pitch, near DRAM-class density, using only i-line tools.

title: Taylor-wire woven memory: glass-coated amorphous microwires as bistable bits
idea: Revive the Taylor (1924) and Ulitovsky (1950s) process, which draws glass-coated amorphous Fe-Si-B microwires with near-perfect square hysteresis (a large Barkhausen jump), and weave them with copper word wires like a 1960s core plane. Each crossing segment flips only on coincident currents and gives a sharp sense pulse, and the bit pitch is set by wire diameter and weave rather than lithography.
why: No EUV and no masks at all; abundant Fe, Si, B and glass; textile-mill manufacturing in the US; infinite endurance, nonvolatile cold working tier; claims ~100x lower capex per bit than a fab, at lower density.

title: Vertical Bloch-line memory revived in rare-earth-free barium hexaferrite
idea: Revive Konishi's 1983 vertical-Bloch-line memory, which stores bits as pairs of Bloch lines inside stripe-domain walls, in perpendicular BaFe12O19 hexaferrite (Ba and Fe are abundant) instead of gadolinium-gallium garnets. A 1 um i-line pattern hosts bits about 10x finer than itself.
why: No EUV, yet bit density below the lithography limit; nonvolatile; no Gd, Ga, Hf or W; claims 10-30x density over the litho node used, as a nonvolatile memory tier.

title: Sonic-film memory: strain pulses address bits instead of transistors
idea: Revive Sperry's 1960s sonic-film memory: an AlN transducer launches a GHz strain pulse along a magnetostrictive Fe-Co strip, and a global current pulse writes only where the strain pulse is at that instant (magnetoelastic coincidence). The inverse effect reads the bit back, so a bit's location is set by time of flight.
why: No EUV, no per-bit transistors and no decoders (fact 7: periphery); no Hf or W; addressing logic shrinks to timers; claims 5x less periphery area per bit.

title: Anodized-alumina pores as self-ordered capacitor holes, no plasma etch
idea: Revive 1960s anodized thin-film capacitor chemistry: anodize an aluminum layer over the transistor array so self-ordered hexagonal pores (40 nm pitch, aspect ratio 100+:1) grow without lithography or plasma etch. The pores are lined with ALD TiN/Al2O3-TiO2/TiN, and each DUV-defined landing pad collects several pores in parallel.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) with no EUV, no PFAS high-aspect-ratio etch (the costliest DRAM etch) and no Hf, using a water-based oxalic acid electrolyte; claims aspect ratio >100 at near-zero etch cost.

title: Atanasoff capacitor-drum regeneration on Gen-10.5 display glass panels
idea: Revive the 1942 Atanasoff-Berry 'jogged' capacitor memory as huge-area arrays on 3 m display glass: LTPS TFTs and metal-insulator-metal capacitors at 1.5 um design rules, with ABC-style continuous regeneration by row-parallel sense circuits at the panel edge.
why: No EUV, no Czochralski wafers or quartz crucibles (glass is made from sand), and it reuses idle panel fabs; ~9 m2 per substrate offsets the low density; claims 5-10x lower capex per bit for bulk, slower tiers.

title: CCD serial memory revived in idle CMOS image-sensor fabs
idea: Revive Fairchild/Intel's 1975 CCD memory: build buried-channel two-phase CCD loops, where data recirculates and is regenerated every lap, at 65-90 nm on image-sensor lines, as a sequential tier for weight streaming and KV-cache scans.
why: No EUV, no capacitor pillars, no Hf or W; uses mature 300 mm sensor capacity at ~4F2 per bit at relaxed F; claims 3x cheaper per bit than DDR for streaming access.

title: Apollo rope memory reborn: laser-programmed inductive ROM for frozen weights
idea: Revive Apollo core-rope ROM, where each bit is whether a sense wire threads or bypasses a shared core: on a mature-node die with ferrite micro-transformers, a laser-cut or inkjet last-metal layer sets the threading choice after fab, so one die type can store any frozen model's weights.
why: No EUV, no per-model masks, no refresh, and no DRAM bits spent on weights; uses only Fe, Ni and Cu; claims to free 50-80% of inference DRAM capacity for KV cache.

title: Qimonda deep-trench DRAM revived with polysilicon and oxynitride only
idea: Revive the trench-capacitor DRAM abandoned with Qimonda (2009) and IBM eDRAM: deep substrate trenches with doped polysilicon electrodes, an oxide-nitride dielectric and buried-strap access, built on 28-40 nm ArF immersion lines in US foundries.
why: No EUV, no Hf/Zr and minimal tungsten, on existing US mature capacity; claims US DRAM output from existing fabs within 2 years, at ~3x the cost per bit of the leading edge.

title: Zone-melting recrystallization stacks DRAM tiers without new wafers
idea: Revive MIT Lincoln Lab's 1980s zone-melting recrystallization: deposit amorphous silicon over a finished DRAM tier, melt it with a scanned line laser seeded through vias to form single-crystal islands, and build the next DUV-patterned tier on it, repeating for 8-16 tiers.
why: Density comes from tiers rather than EUV pitch (facts 2, 4), and no tier needs its own Czochralski wafer (quartz crucible) or bonding; claims 8x bits per wafer from 16 DUV tiers at 2x pitch.

title: Interference lithography with neon-free solid-state lasers for array lines
idea: Revive 1970s holographic-grating interference lithography for the periodic DRAM array: two or four beams from a 213 nm fifth-harmonic solid-state laser print dense line/space and hole arrays without masks, with DUV steppers used only for trims and periphery.
why: No EUV, no array masks and no neon (ArF/KrF excimer lasers need neon, concentrated in Ukraine); claims 60 nm-pitch arrays for ~10% of an EUV scanner's capital.

title: PFAS-free DNQ-novolac resist revival for periphery layers
idea: Revive 1980s diazonaphthoquinone-novolac i-line resists, which contain no fluorinated photoacid generators, for every periphery and non-critical layer (about half the die), paired with second-hand i-line steppers.
why: PFAS phase-outs threaten chemically amplified resists, while DNQ is PFAS-free and cheap; no EUV; claims 50-60% of resist volume becomes PFAS-free at no cost penalty.

title: Pre-plasma wet etching returns for non-critical DRAM layers
idea: Revive 1970s wet chemical etching (hot phosphoric acid for nitride, buffered HF for oxide, aqueous metal etches with recycled etchant) for coarse layers, replacing fluorocarbon plasma steps that also need helium backside wafer cooling.
why: Cuts PFAS/fluorinated greenhouse-gas use and helium consumption, with no EUV; claims 20-30% fewer plasma steps per wafer.

title: Stencil shadow-mask deposition revived: no resist, no etch, no PFAS
idea: Revive 1960s shadow-mask evaporation with MEMS silicon-nitride stencils held close to the wafer, depositing patterned metals and dielectrics directly for BEOL plates, pads and periphery wiring with no resist and no etch.
why: No EUV, no PFAS resists or etch gases, and almost no chemical waste; claims 3-5 mask-and-etch modules removed per wafer.

title: Copper-oxide rectifier revival: diode-access capacitor crosspoint, stacked tiers
idea: Revive the 1920s cuprous-oxide rectifier as a BEOL p-Cu2O/n-ZnO heterojunction diode in series with a MIM capacitor at each crosspoint, selected coincident-current style like core planes (half-select stays below diode turn-on) and stacked in several DUV-patterned tiers.
why: No access transistor, no tungsten, no Hf and no EUV, using abundant Cu, Zn and O; claims 4F2 per tier over 4 tiers; the honest risk is diode reverse leakage limiting retention.

title: Millipede revived: thermomechanical probes on recyclable Diels-Alder polymer
idea: Revive IBM's abandoned Millipede: arrays of heated silicon cantilever tips write nanometer pits into a thermally reversible Diels-Alder polymer film and read them through the tip's thermal resistance change. The tip arrays are i-line patterned at 50 um pitch while the bits are 10 nm.
why: Density below the lithography limit without EUV; the medium is cheap organic polymer with no metals; a dense nonvolatile capacity tier that offloads cold DRAM pages; claims 1 Tb/in2 at microsecond access.

title: Telephone-exchange Erlang trunking for memory: optical circuit-switched DRAM pools
idea: Revive Bell System Erlang traffic engineering and crossbar exchanges: size rack memory like phone trunks, to the 99.9th-percentile aggregate demand rather than each server's peak, and connect servers to pooled DRAM through MEMS optical circuit switches carrying CXL over optics.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: about 25-30% of cloud DRAM sits stranded, and Erlang provisioning cuts purchased DRAM 20-30% with no new fabs and no EUV.

title: Liberty-ship mini-fabs: identical DUV-only DRAM fabs from used tools
idea: Revive the WWII Liberty-ship approach: freeze one standardized no-EUV DRAM design and fab layout (10k wafers/month, second-hand ArF-immersion scanners, refurbished etch and deposition tools) and have the same crews replicate it quickly across many US states.
why: Capital intensity and time to capacity: no EUV, ~1/5 the capex of a leading-edge fab, built in 18 months; claims to raise the US share of bits from 1-2% to ~5%.

title: Mandatory second-sourcing revived for a no-EUV American DRAM process
idea: Revive the 1960s-80s defense rule that every critical chip has a licensed second source: require CHIPS-funded DRAM designs to be built on an open no-EUV process licensed to at least two US mature-node foundries.
why: U.S. manufacturability and resilience: spreads output across existing DUV capacity and avoids the single-supplier EUV chokepoint.

title: Reed-relay access DRAM: NEMS switches with zero off-leakage
idea: Revive the reed relays of the 1965 Bell No.1 ESS as BEOL NEMS contact switches that connect each storage capacitor to its bitline. When the switch is open, an air gap gives effectively zero leakage, so a small planar MIM capacitor holds charge for hours.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): refresh nearly disappears, so the capacitor can shrink to ~1 fF in flat MIM instead of high-aspect-ratio pillars (fact 1); BEOL at DUV pitch with no EUV; TiN/SiC materials, no Hf.

title: Shockley four-layer diode revived as thyristor RAM cell
idea: Revive Shockley's 1956 four-layer diode and the abandoned 2000s T-RAM: a vertical PNPN thyristor with a capacitively coupled gate latches regeneratively and stores a bit without a capacitor, built at 40 nm DUV pitch.
why: No capacitor (fact 1), no Hf, no W pillars and no EUV; reads in under 5 ns at high current; claims SRAM-like speed in a ~8F2 DUV footprint.

title: Wartime tungsten scrap reclamation feeds domestic fab tungsten chemistry
idea: Revive 1940s cemented-carbide scrap reclamation (the zinc process) and capture tungsten from WF6 exhaust and chamber cleans, converting both into fab-grade WF6 and W targets inside the US for DUV-only memory lines.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): closes the loop on fab tungsten; claims 50%+ of fab W from recycled sources.

title: IBM-style memory leasing: makers own bits, reclaim and redeploy
idea: Revive IBM's 1950s practice of leasing core memory instead of selling it: DRAM makers lease modules by the GB-month, keep ownership, and are paid to reclaim, retest and redeploy them into second-life tiers.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: aligns incentives to stretch module life from ~5 to ~10 years, effectively raising supply; no EUV; claims 10-20% more bit-years per wafer.
